title: The game is the living world you described in Part I — the loop is just its first mile
unblocks: loop bar wording, all zone work
detail: You already ruled this in chat (2026-07-30, forklift session) — this card is the confirmation tap for the record. The Erenshor-style persistent zoned world IS the design you recorded from question 16 onward (zone bands, city-fee death, geographic quests, living hubs, collectathon endgame). The loop milestone is the first playable mile of that world, not a separate run-game. Nothing in the register needs amending.

title: Name it a pillar: zones intertwine — glimpses of your future self are hidden everywhere
detail: Your call from the forklift session: zones keep a general level progression, but deliberately contain cross-band pockets — an endgame corner inside a starter zone (walk in, get one-shot, learn and remember), a high-level dungeon under a low-level city. Your words: 'we can potentially score a lot here.' This card asks: is this a named pillar (protected, always considered in zone work) or just a normal rule?

title: Name it a pillar: everything in the world has a reason a villager could tell you
unblocks: world_filler direction sessions, all placement work
detail: Your call: the world must never feel like objectives placed on a map. Every camp, dungeon, rare route, and road has an in-world reason discoverable by looking at it. Working test for any placement: 'what is this doing here?' should have an answer a villager could give. Wolves denning above the sheep farms passes; 'a level-8 camp because this is the level-8 area' fails.

title: Night and weather may never make the game harder to see or heavier to run
detail: Your recorded pet peeve turned into a standing guardrail: whenever day/night or weather get built (both deferred), night must never be a visibility tax that makes grinding feel bad, and weather must never cost framerate. Atmosphere only ever adds. Adopting this now means no future session can build a darkness-tax night by default.

title: Adopt the aliveness test: organic enemies first, loot worth reading second, sound you never mute third
detail: Your own definition from today, in order: (1) enemies and camps read as organic places, not generic placements — the prerequisite for caring at all; (2) drops that make you stop and read the stats; (3) music and sfx good enough that you don't mute them (already passed — you historically mute game music and haven't muted this). 'When I want to play the game, that is when it feels alive.' This orders the first-slice work.
